narrative:
The model estimates a 34.0% chance that you will fail your final year. That is not a certainty, but it is high enough that the school’s rule treats you as needing remedial courses. The strongest reason for this prediction is that you do not want to continue to higher education. This was the most influential factor and it pushed the prediction toward failing; among students who passed, every comparison case wanted higher education. Two other factors worked in your favor. You have no past class failures, which matched the passing average and pushed toward passing. Your commute of 30–60 minutes also counted as a favorable factor in the model, even though most passing students travel under 15 minutes. Those positive signals were not enough to offset the main concern.

To improve your chances, focus first on building a clear plan for continuing education after school, since this was the largest warning sign. Also reduce your eight absences, well above the passing average of 3.78, and increase weekly study time: you study under two hours, while most passing students study two to five hours. You also lack family educational support and home internet, unlike most passing students, so ask teachers or the school for structured support and use school resources. These steps address the concerns the model weighted most and can make failure less likely.
